CausalChain: HCC cells secrete exosomal PKM2 -> Exosomal PKM2 is internalized by macrophage precursors and Kupffer cells -> Upregulation of PFKFB3 enhances glycolysis in TAMs -> Increased glycolytic flux leads to PD-L1 upregulation and M2 polarization -> Immunosuppressive TAMs inhibit CD8+ T cell function and promote tumor progression -> Blocking PKM2 uptake or inhibiting PFKFB3 reverses M2 polarization to M1 phenotype -> Enhanced T cell activity leads to improved tumor control
Hypothesis: Targeting the exosomal PKM2–PFKFB3 axis in tumor-associated macrophages will reprogram them from a pro-tumoral M2 phenotype to an antitumoral M1 state, thereby enhancing CD8+ T cell-mediated immunity and improving the efficacy of immune checkpoint blockade in hepatocellular carcinoma.
Abstract: We propose that metabolic reprogramming via glycolytic enzymes plays a pivotal role in directing tumor‐associated macrophage (TAM) polarization within the hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) microenvironment. Specifically, HCC cells release exosomes containing PKM2 that, when internalized by infiltrating monocytes and tissue‐resident Kupffer cells, upregulate PFKFB3 and enhance glycolysis, leading to increased PD‐L1 expression and M2 polarization. This immunosuppressive switch impedes cytotoxic CD8+ T cell activity and promotes tumor progression. We hypothesize that pharmacologically inhibiting exosomal PKM2 uptake or its downstream glycolytic effector PFKFB3 will reprogram TAMs toward an M1 phenotype and sensitize HCC to immune checkpoint therapy.
